results.content: # How to Integrate FHIR APIs with Epic, Cerner, and Other Major EHRs. Integrating FHIR APIs with major EHR systems like Epic and Cerner is challenging due to each vendor's unique implementations, workflows, and technical nuances. * **EHR-Specific FHIR Variations**: Epic uses SMART on FHIR with strict OAuth2 protocols, while Cerner supports both FHIR R4 and older DSTU2 versions. * **Testing Challenges**: Sandbox environments often differ from production systems, requiring extensive testing to handle edge cases, rate limits, and real-world data complexities. Working with Epic's FHIR implementation comes with its own set of challenges, requiring tailored strategies for authentication and patient data management. Nextech provides FHIR R4 endpoints alongside custom REST APIs. Testing these endpoints is crucial to understand their specific resource support and authentication requirements. Some systems even adopt a hybrid approach, using FHIR endpoints for standard resources and proprietary APIs for accessing custom fields or specialty-specific data. Custom EHR integrations often demand robust data transformation layers to handle inconsistent field mappings and non-standard extensions. After tackling authentication and data mapping, the next hurdle in achieving smooth multi-EHR integration is managing FHIR profiles and extensions. However, the implementation of these extensions can differ significantly between FHIR STU3 and R4 versions, requiring version-specific handling. Building on earlier discussions about authentication and data mapping, let’s dive into some practical tips for managing version conflicts, normalizing data, and tackling testing challenges in FHIR integrations. Epic’s capability statements typically outline supported FHIR versions for each resource type, while Cerner’s may need extra testing to confirm compatibility. ### What are the main differences when integrating FHIR APIs with Epic and Cerner EHR systems? results.content: You will learn how to integrate wearable device data into EHRs with AI intelligence using patterns that already work in hospitals: FHIR reads and writes, SMART on FHIR (S*ubstitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies on FHIR*) launch, and HL7 v2 (*Health Level Seven version 2*) event feeds. + Typical wiring: device data → Pub/Sub → Dataflow normalization → Cloud Healthcare API (FHIR store) → EHR via FHIR REST; AI runs in Vertex AI and posts risk scores or summaries to `Observation` or `DiagnosticReport`. results.title: FHIR R4 and USCDI: What’s the current state; what mandated changes are coming next - Greenlight Health Data Solutions, Inc.
results.content: # FHIR R4 and USCDI: What’s the current state; what mandated changes are coming next. To that end, Greenlight customers often ask specifically about FHIR R4 and USCDI. They want to know if the R4 data is up to date regarding the USCDI standard mandated by the **Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology** (ONCHIT, usually abbreviated as just ONC). FHIR defines what medical record data goes where in the json file that gets shared by EHRs and health facilities. * **USCDI** (US Core Data for Interoperability) is a list of the minimum data types which must be shared if an EHR is going to be “certified” as interoperable, and the facility using it is going to be eligible for the CMS reimbursement bonuses available only to certified EHR users. EHRs must be sharing using USCDI version 3’s rules, by January 1, 2026, to stay “certified.”. The illustration below shows how ONC progresses through USCDI versions, and how this relates to what you can expect in FHIR R4 data from most EHRs today. What does this mean for a customer getting FHIR R4 data from the Greenlight platform? * Greenlight retrieves all the FHIR R4 resources the EHR makes available. * As we approach January 1, 2026, EHRs will begin to add the data required under USCDI v3. As EHRs add these “to be” required data fields, Greenlight is monitoring for these additions and will retrieve any new FHIR resources and any new data elements that show up in those resources. * By January 1, 2026, ONC may propose another version of FHIR (beyond R4) and maybe the next “required” version of USCDI, but they will give the EHRs months (18-24, typically) to implement that change. * Greenlight always gets all the FHIR R4 data made available by the EHR and by the facility. * As the EHRs share more data (complying with USCDI v3 by Jan 1, 2026), Greenlight will get and share that data through our normal API process. Please **contact us** with any questions regarding compliance with FHIR R4 and USCDI requirements, or to discuss how you can advance the electronic health data revolution in your organization.

results.title: What is FHIR and Why It Matters in EHRs? – 75Health
results.content: At 75Health, we **follow and support FHIR standards** for seamless data exchange. **FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources)** is a **new data standard developed by HL7 (Health Level 7)** to facilitate the exchange of healthcare information in a timely manner. When it comes to Electronic Health Records (EHRs), having the right data at the right time can save lives. FHIR allows EHRs to gather up-to-date information from different sources labs, pharmacies and other hospitals, so healthcare providers always see the latest patient records. By organizing data into reusable resources (such as allergies, medications, lab results), FHIR enables EHRs to show relevant clinical info helping doctors make quicker, more informed decisions. FHIR-compatible EHRs can share data with patient apps. FHIR makes EHRs work better with AI systems, tools that help make decisions, software for billing, and apps on phones. FHIR supports strict privacy controls, ensuring that EHRs can share data securely while staying compliant with global healthcare standards.
